explanations.explanation: Everyone, friend. Paul, the apostle writing to Timothy, doesn't draw a fence around this prayer list. He says petitions, prayers, intercessions and thanksgiving are to be offered for everyone (1 Timothy 2:1). That's a longer list than the line outside my bakery on a Saturday morning.

I see why you'd pick it, but Paul never narrows the list here. He says the prayers are to be offered for everyone (1 Timothy 2:1). That's a lot bigger than one group, and it's the neighbor you wave at and the one you pretend not to see in the driveway.

Paul doesn't mention elders in this verse at all. He says the petitions, prayers, intercessions and thanksgiving are for everyone (1 Timothy 2:1). That includes the elders, but it sure doesn't stop there. Everyone means everyone, friend.

explanations.answer: Kings and all those in authority
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Right after saying everyone, Paul names kings and all those in authority (1 Timothy 2:2). Think about that for a second. Praying for the people in charge is on Paul's list, and I bet that's a stretch some days.

Widows and orphans aren't named in this passage. After saying everyone, Paul points to one group, and it's kings and all those in authority (1 Timothy 2:2). Good heart on that answer, though. It just belongs to a different list.

Paul doesn't name prophets or teachers here. The group he points to is kings and all those in authority (1 Timothy 2:2). He's talking about the folks holding the steering wheel, friend. I'd say that's a group that could use a prayer or two.

True, friend. Paul says to pray for kings and all those in authority, “…so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity.” (1 Timothy 2:2). The text gives that reason itself, so we don't have to guess. Tranquil and quiet. Somebody write that on my oven door.

This one is actually true, and Paul says it plainly. He wants prayers for kings and all those in authority, “…so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity.” (1 Timothy 2:2). Every part of the statement is in the verse. Easy to second-guess it when it sounds this peaceful, friend.

Good and pleasing, that's Paul's word for it. He says praying for everyone, kings included, is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior (1 Timothy 2:3). Two words, and no fine print. That's about as clear as a recipe gets.

Praying for kings might feel bold, I'll give you that. But Paul doesn't use those words. He calls it good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior (1 Timothy 2:3). Nothing risky in his description, friend.

Paul never says hard or costly here. He says this is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior (1 Timothy 2:3). Some prayers might feel heavy to carry, but that's not the word on the page. The page says good and pleasing.

Not quite, friend, and Paul says the opposite. God our Savior wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). There's no short list in that verse. The word he uses is everyone.

False, and the verse is clear. Paul says God our Savior wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4). It's not a select few. Everyone is the word, and that's why the prayer list is so big.
The man Christ Jesus, that's exactly what Paul says. There is one God, and one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5). One, not a committee. That's Paul's whole point, friend.

Moses was Israel's leader, so I get the thought. But Paul names a different person as the one mediator between God and men. It's the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Moses doesn't show up anywhere in this passage.

Aaron was Moses' brother, appointed to serve as priest (Exodus 28:1), so that's a thoughtful guess. Paul still names someone else here. He says there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Aaron isn't in this passage.

Ransom is the word, friend. Paul says Christ Jesus gave Himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:6). Jesus used that word about Himself too: “…to give His life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45). It's a big word, and it's the heart of this whole passage.

Jesus taught plenty, but that's not the word Paul uses. He says Christ Jesus gave Himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:6). A ransom is a price paid, and it's a much bigger thing than a lesson. Jesus said it Himself: “…to give His life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45).

Paul doesn't call it a warning. He says Christ Jesus gave Himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:6). Jesus said the same about Himself: “…to give His life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45). Ransom is the word that fits the blank.

Anger or dissension, that's what Paul says to leave out. He wants the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension (1 Timothy 2:8). Hands up, grudges down. I've burned a batch or two when I was grumpy, so I get it.

Paul doesn't mention music or singing in this verse. He wants the men to pray with holy hands lifted up, without anger or dissension (1 Timothy 2:8). The thing to leave out is the fighting, friend. The tune is up to you.
Fasting and sackcloth don't come up in this verse. Paul wants the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension (1 Timothy 2:8). That's the thing he says to leave behind.

Good deeds, that's the one. Paul wants the women to be adorned with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God (1 Timothy 2:10). Braids, gold, pearls and expensive clothes get set aside for this. Good deeds are the outfit he points to.

Prayer is a good thing, but it's not the word in this verse. Paul says the women are to be adorned with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God (1 Timothy 2:10). It's what they do that he points to. Long prayers aren't named here.

Fasting and tears don't show up here. Paul says the women are to be adorned with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God (1 Timothy 2:10). That's the contrast he draws with braids, gold, pearls and expensive clothes.

explanations.answer: Teach or exercise authority over a man
explanations.explanation: That's the pair Paul names. He says, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.” (1 Timothy 2:12). Both things are in the same sentence, so it's one to read slowly. Nice and careful, friend.

explanations.answer: Own land or run a business of her own
explanations.explanation: Owning land and running a business aren't in this passage. Paul says, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.” (1 Timothy 2:12). Those two things are the pair he names. Nothing about land or business shows up.

explanations.answer: Travel or trade in the market alone
explanations.explanation: Travel and trade don't come up here. What Paul says is, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.” (1 Timothy 2:12). The pair is teaching and exercising authority over a man. The market isn't mentioned.

True. Paul says, “For Adam was formed first, and then Eve.” (1 Timothy 2:13). Adam, the first man, and Eve, the first woman, go all the way back to the beginning (Genesis 2:22). Paul states it plainly and I'll leave it as he says it.
This one's actually true. Paul says, “For Adam was formed first, and then Eve.” (1 Timothy 2:13). Adam was the first man, and Eve came after (Genesis 2:22). It's right there in the verse, friend.

Paul actually says the opposite. He writes, “And it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression.” (1 Timothy 2:14). The verse says Adam was not the one deceived. It names the woman, friend, so it's one to read twice.

False, and you read it right. Paul says, “And it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression.” (1 Timothy 2:14). He names the woman as the one deceived. Careful reading, friend.

Faith is the word. Paul says women will be saved through childbearing, “…if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control.” (1 Timothy 2:15). Faith leads the list, and it's the first thing he names. Keep an eye on that little word if, friend.

Wisdom is a good thing, but it's not on Paul's list in this verse. He says, “…if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control.” (1 Timothy 2:15). The first word in that list is faith.

Patience is a fine thing, and I've needed plenty of it waiting on a slow oven. But it's not what Paul names. He says, “…if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control.” (1 Timothy 2:15). The word for the blank is faith.
